title: Baptism in the Spirit and Spiritual Gifts
summary: What the Bible teaches about the baptism in the Holy Spirit, speaking in tongues and the gifts of the Spirit, with each tradition's view set out fairly.
description: Few subjects stir more discussion among Nigerian Christians than the baptism in the Holy Spirit and spiritual gifts. This course studies Pentecost and the other outpourings in Acts, explains the Pentecostal, Holiness, Baptist and Reformed understandings of Spirit baptism, surveys the gifts listed in the New Testament, examines tongues and prophecy, and gives Paul's guidelines for using gifts in love and order.
objectives: Study the outpourings of the Spirit in Acts
Present fairly the main views of Spirit baptism
Survey the gifts of the Spirit in the New Testament
Explain the biblical guidelines for tongues and prophecy
Present the continuationist and cessationist views fairly
outcomes: Describe what happened at Pentecost and in Samaria, Caesarea and Ephesus
Compare the 'subsequent' and 'at conversion' views of Spirit baptism
List and explain the main spiritual gifts
Apply Paul's rules for orderly worship
Help believers discover and use their gifts in love

modules.title: The Day of Pentecost
modules.intro: The promise of the Father was fulfilled at Pentecost. This week we study Acts 2 and its meaning.

lessons.title: The promise of the Father
lessons.body:
Before His ascension Jesus told the disciples to "wait for the promise of the Father": "ye shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost not many days hence" (Acts 1:4-5). The purpose was power for witness "unto the uttermost part of the earth" (1:8).

The disciples obeyed: "These all continued with one accord in prayer and supplication" (1:14). About 120 believers waited in Jerusalem (1:15).

Pentecost was a Jewish harvest feast fifty days after Passover. It was fitting that the Spirit came on the day of firstfruits, beginning the great harvest of souls.

lessons.title: Wind, fire and tongues
lessons.body:
"And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind... And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance" (Acts 2:2-4).

The tongues were real languages: visitors from many nations heard "every man in his own language" the wonderful works of God (2:6-11).

Some mocked, saying they were drunk (2:13). Peter explained that this was what Joel had prophesied: "I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh" (2:16-17).

lessons.title: Peter's sermon and the promise for all
lessons.body:
Filled with the Spirit, Peter preached Christ crucified and risen. The people were "pricked in their heart" and asked what to do (Acts 2:37).

"Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost. For the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the Lord our God shall call" (2:38-39).

About three thousand were saved that day (2:41). The church that followed was marked by the apostles' teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, prayer and generosity (2:42-47).

terms.def: The Jewish harvest feast fifty days after Passover, when the Spirit was poured out.
Jesus' name for the promised gift of the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:4).
The room in Jerusalem where the disciples gathered and prayed before Pentecost.
Divided flames that rested on each believer at Pentecost.
Languages the speakers had not learned, given by the Spirit.
The Spirit Himself, promised to all who repent and believe (Acts 2:38).

texts.teaches: The disciples would be baptized with the Holy Ghost not many days later.
They were all filled with the Holy Ghost and spoke with other tongues.
God will pour out His Spirit upon all flesh in the last days.
Repent and be baptized, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.
The promise is to you, your children and all that are afar off.

summary: Jesus commanded the disciples to wait for the promised Spirit.
At Pentecost the Spirit came with wind, fire and tongues.
The tongues were real languages declaring God's works.
The promise of the Spirit is for all whom the Lord calls.

questions.q: How many days after Passover was Pentecost?
What did the visitors hear at Pentecost?
options: The wonderful works of God in their own languages

questions.q: Which prophet did Peter quote?
About how many were saved after Peter's sermon?

modules.title: Outpourings in Acts
modules.intro: Acts records further outpourings of the Spirit. This week we study Samaria, Caesarea and Ephesus and what they show.

lessons.title: Samaria (Acts 8)
lessons.body:
Philip preached Christ in Samaria; many believed and were baptized (Acts 8:5-12). Yet the Holy Ghost "was fallen upon none of them" until Peter and John came and laid hands on them, "and they received the Holy Ghost" (8:15-17).

Simon the sorcerer saw something visible happen and offered money for the power. Peter rebuked him: "thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money" (8:18-20).

Pentecostals see here a separation between believing and receiving the Spirit. Others explain the delay as unique: God joining the despised Samaritans to the Jerusalem church through the apostles.

lessons.title: Caesarea (Acts 10)
lessons.body:
Peter preached to Cornelius, a Gentile, and his household. "While Peter yet spake these words, the Holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word" (Acts 10:44). The Jewish believers were astonished, "For they heard them speak with tongues, and magnify God" (10:46).

Here the Spirit came at the moment of faith, even before water baptism (10:47-48).

Peter later said God "put no difference between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith" (15:8-9). The outpouring proved that Gentiles were fully accepted by God.

lessons.title: Ephesus (Acts 19)
lessons.body:
Paul met about twelve disciples in Ephesus and asked, "Have ye received the Holy Ghost since ye believed?" They had not even heard of the Holy Ghost; they knew only John's baptism (Acts 19:2-3).

Paul explained that John pointed to Jesus. They were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, and when Paul laid hands on them, "the Holy Ghost came on them; and they spake with tongues, and prophesied" (19:5-6).

Pentecostals use Paul's question to show that receiving the Spirit can follow believing. Others note that these men were disciples of John, not yet Christians, and received the Spirit when they believed in Jesus.

terms.def: Placing hands on a person in prayer, often linked with receiving the Spirit or commissioning.
Trying to buy or sell spiritual things, named after Simon the sorcerer.
The Roman centurion whose household received the Spirit as Peter preached.
Followers of John the Baptist who had not yet heard the full gospel of Jesus.
A name for the outpouring at Cornelius' house, showing Gentiles accepted.
The difference between what Acts records happening and what it commands for all.

texts.teaches: Peter and John laid hands on the Samaritans and they received the Holy Ghost.
The gift of God cannot be purchased with money.
The Holy Ghost fell on all who heard the word at Cornelius' house.
Paul asked, 'Have ye received the Holy Ghost since ye believed?'
The Ephesian disciples spoke with tongues and prophesied when the Spirit came.

summary: In Samaria the Spirit came after baptism, through the apostles' hands.
At Caesarea the Spirit fell as Gentiles heard and believed.
At Ephesus disciples of John received the Spirit after believing in Jesus.
Christians differ on whether these patterns are normal for all believers.

questions.q: Who tried to buy the power to give the Spirit?
At Cornelius' house, when did the Spirit fall?
What baptism did the Ephesian disciples know?
What does 'descriptive' mean in reading Acts?

modules.title: Views of Spirit Baptism
modules.intro: This week we set out fairly the main ways Christians understand the baptism in the Holy Spirit.

lessons.title: The Pentecostal and Holiness view
lessons.body:
Classical Pentecostals, including the Assemblies of God and many Nigerian Pentecostal churches, teach that the baptism in the Holy Spirit is a distinct experience after conversion, giving power for service, with **speaking in tongues as the initial physical evidence**.

Holiness Pentecostals, including Deeper Life Bible Church, teach three experiences: salvation, then sanctification as a second work of grace, then the baptism in the Holy Spirit with tongues. Deeper Life stresses that a holy heart is the proper vessel for the Spirit's power.

They point to Acts 2, 8, 10 and 19, to Paul's question in Acts 19:2, and to Jesus' words in Luke 11:13 about the Father giving the Spirit to those who ask.

lessons.title: The Baptist and Reformed view
lessons.body:
Most Baptists and Reformed Christians teach that every believer is baptized by the Spirit at conversion: "For by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body" (1 Corinthians 12:13). "If any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his" (Romans 8:9).

They see the events in Acts as unique, marking the gospel's spread to new groups: Jews (Acts 2), Samaritans (8), Gentiles (10) and John's disciples (19), in line with Acts 1:8.

They stress repeated **fillings** with the Spirit for power and boldness (Acts 4:31; Ephesians 5:18), and teach that tongues are one gift among many, not given to all: "do all speak with tongues?" (1 Corinthians 12:30).

lessons.title: Seeking the fullness of the Spirit
lessons.body:
Charismatic and 'Third Wave' Christians take a middle path: they welcome the Spirit's gifts and fresh experiences of power, but do not insist on tongues as the required evidence.

All the traditions agree on much:

- Every Christian has the Spirit.
- Believers need continual filling and empowering for witness.
- The Spirit's work should produce holiness and love, not pride.
- God gives the Spirit to those who ask (Luke 11:13).

Whatever your tradition, seek God's fullness humbly, test experiences by Scripture, and do not despise believers who understand this differently.

terms.def: The Spirit's coming upon or immersing a believer; understood either as a second experience or as part of conversion.
The teaching that Spirit baptism is a distinct experience after conversion.
The Pentecostal teaching that tongues are the first physical sign of Spirit baptism.
A fresh empowering of the Spirit, which may be repeated.
A Christian in a historic denomination who embraces spiritual gifts and experiences.
The Holiness Pentecostal sequence of salvation, sanctification and Spirit baptism.

texts.teaches: By one Spirit we are all baptized into one body.
If any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of His.
The heavenly Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him.
Paul asks, 'Do all speak with tongues?'
The praying believers were filled again and spoke with boldness.

summary: Pentecostals teach Spirit baptism after conversion, with tongues as initial evidence.
Holiness Pentecostals, including Deeper Life, place it after salvation and sanctification.
Baptists and Reformed teach Spirit baptism at conversion, with later fillings.
All agree believers need the Spirit's continual filling for holiness and witness.

questions.q: What do classical Pentecostals call the initial evidence of Spirit baptism?
Which text do Baptists cite for Spirit baptism at conversion?
Deeper Life teaches which sequence?
On what do all traditions agree?
options: Believers need the Spirit's continual filling
The Spirit is not for today

modules.title: The Gifts of the Spirit
modules.intro: The Spirit gives gifts to every believer. This week we survey the gifts and how to discover and use them.

lessons.title: One Spirit, many gifts
lessons.body:
"Now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit. And there are differences of administrations, but the same Lord. And there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God which worketh all in all" (1 Corinthians 12:4-6).

The body has many members, each needed: "the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee" (12:21). No gift makes a person superior or inferior.

The gifts are given "to every man to profit withal" (12:7), distributed "as he will" (12:11). We do not choose our gifts, but we may "covet earnestly the best gifts" for the good of the church (12:31).

lessons.title: The lists of gifts
lessons.body:
The New Testament gives several lists:

- **1 Corinthians 12:8-10**: word of wisdom, word of knowledge, faith, gifts of healing, working of miracles, prophecy, discerning of spirits, kinds of tongues, interpretation of tongues.
- **Romans 12:6-8**: prophecy, ministry (serving), teaching, exhortation, giving, ruling (leading), showing mercy.
- **Ephesians 4:11**: apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers, given "for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry" (4:12).
- **1 Peter 4:10-11**: speaking gifts and serving gifts.

The lists are examples, not a complete catalogue.

lessons.title: Discovering and using your gift
lessons.body:
"As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God" (1 Peter 4:10).

Ways to discover your gifts:

1. Pray and offer yourself for service (Romans 12:1).
2. Serve in different areas and notice where God blesses your work.
3. Listen to mature believers who observe you.
4. Look for a desire and burden God has placed in you.

Paul told Timothy, "Neglect not the gift that is in thee" and "stir up the gift of God" (1 Timothy 4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6). Gifts grow as they are used faithfully.

terms.def: Greek for 'grace-gifts': gifts freely given by the Spirit.
A Spirit-given insight into how to act rightly in a situation.
A Spirit-given understanding of truth or facts for the good of others.
The ability to tell whether something is from God, man or demons.
The gift of encouraging and urging others toward faithfulness.
The gifts of apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers (Ephesians 4:11).

texts.teaches: There are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit.
No member of the body can say it has no need of another.
Believers have gifts differing according to the grace given.
Leadership gifts equip the saints for the work of the ministry.
Use your gift to serve one another as good stewards of God's grace.

summary: One Spirit gives many different gifts to every believer.
The New Testament gives several lists of gifts as examples.
Gifts are for building up the body, not for status.
Discover your gifts by serving, praying and listening to mature believers.

questions.q: What does charismata mean?
Which passage lists apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers?
Who decides which gifts a believer receives?
What did Paul tell Timothy to do with his gift?
options: Stir it up and not neglect it

modules.title: Tongues, Prophecy and Order
modules.intro: Paul gave the Corinthians careful guidance on tongues and prophecy. This week we study it, and the debate over whether all gifts continue today.

lessons.title: The more excellent way
lessons.body:
Between his teaching on gifts (1 Corinthians 12) and on their use (14), Paul writes about love (13). "Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal" (13:1).

Gifts without love are nothing. Love "suffereth long, and is kind... seeketh not her own" (13:4-5). Gifts are temporary; "charity never faileth" (13:8).

The Corinthians had many gifts but were divided, proud and immoral (1:7, 11; 5:1). Spiritual gifts are not proof of spiritual maturity. Fruit is.

lessons.title: Tongues and prophecy in the church
lessons.body:
Paul valued tongues: "I thank my God, I speak with tongues more than ye all" (1 Corinthians 14:18). Tongues build up the speaker (14:4) and are a sign to unbelievers (14:22).

But in church he preferred prophecy, which builds up everyone: "he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort" (14:3).

His rules for church meetings:

- Tongues in public must be interpreted, by two or three at most, in turn (14:27-28).
- Prophets speak two or three, and others judge what is said (14:29).
- "Let all things be done decently and in order" (14:40).
- "Forbid not to speak with tongues" (14:39).

lessons.title: Do all the gifts continue today?
lessons.body:
**Continuationists**, including Pentecostals, charismatics and many evangelicals, believe all the gifts continue until Christ returns. They note that 1 Corinthians 13:10 speaks of gifts ceasing "when that which is perfect is come", which they take to mean Christ's return.

**Cessationists**, including many Reformed and some Baptist Christians, believe the sign gifts such as tongues, prophecy and healing miracles ended with the apostles, having confirmed their message (Hebrews 2:3-4), and that the completed Scripture is now our sufficient guide.

Both must test everything: "Despise not prophesyings. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good" (1 Thessalonians 5:20-21). No prophecy may add to or contradict Scripture, and false prophets must be exposed (1 John 4:1).

terms.def: The King James word for self-giving love (Greek agape).
Building up others in faith and holiness.
The Spirit-given ability to make known the meaning of a message in tongues.
Speaking a Spirit-given message to strengthen, encourage and comfort.
Paul's rule for the conduct of worship (1 Corinthians 14:40).
What causes gifts to cease (1 Corinthians 13:10), read as Christ's return or the completed Scripture.

texts.teaches: Tongues without love are like sounding brass.
Prophecy speaks to edification, exhortation and comfort.
Tongues in church should be two or three in turn, with interpretation.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.

summary: Love is the more excellent way; gifts without love are nothing.
Paul preferred prophecy in church because it builds up all.
Tongues in church must be interpreted; all must be done in order.
Continuationists and cessationists differ, but all must test everything by Scripture.

questions.q: Which chapter comes between Paul's teaching on gifts and their use?
Why did Paul prefer prophecy in church?
What must accompany public tongues in church?
What do cessationists believe?
options: Sign gifts ended with the apostles
There are no spiritual gifts at all

short.q: What happened on the Day of Pentecost?
short.model: With a sound like wind and tongues of fire, the believers were filled with the Holy Ghost and spoke in other languages the wonderful works of God.

short.q: Summarise the classical Pentecostal view of Spirit baptism.
short.model: A distinct experience after conversion giving power for service, with speaking in tongues as the initial evidence.

short.q: Summarise the Baptist and Reformed view of Spirit baptism.
short.model: Every believer is baptized by the Spirit at conversion (1 Corinthians 12:13); the events in Acts mark the gospel reaching new groups; believers seek repeated fillings.

short.q: Why are gifts given, according to 1 Corinthians 12?
short.model: To profit and build up the whole body of Christ, not for personal status.

short.q: Give three of Paul's rules for tongues and prophecy in church.
short.model: Public tongues must be interpreted; two or three speak in turn; prophecy is judged; all is done decently and in order.
Continuationists believe all gifts continue until Christ returns; cessationists believe sign gifts ended with the apostles. Both must test everything by Scripture.

lists.q: List five of the nine gifts in 1 Corinthians 12:8-10.
List the four places in Acts where the Spirit came on new groups.

assignments.title: Comparing views of Spirit baptism
assignments.prompt: Explain the Pentecostal, Holiness Pentecostal and Baptist views of the baptism in the Holy Spirit. For each, give its key texts and its strongest point. Then explain how believers from these traditions can serve together in love.

assignments.title: Gifts in my church
assignments.prompt: Using 1 Corinthians 12-14 and Romans 12, assess how spiritual gifts are used in your church or fellowship. What is done well? What could be done more in line with Scripture? Suggest three practical improvements.

reading: Gordon D. Fee, God's Empowering Presence
D. A. Carson, Showing the Spirit: A Theological Exposition of 1 Corinthians 12–14
Wayne Grudem (ed.), Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? Four Views
